---
title: Get started
---

Install Console, connect it to your MCP client, and try an analysis.
No Console configuration file is required.

## Install

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), then install Console:

```sh
uv tool install mcp-console
```

Prebuilt packages are available for macOS and Linux on ARM64 and x86-64, and for experimental Windows x64.
Windows users should also follow the [Windows setup instructions](WINDOWS.md#install-and-run).

If Console fails to start on Linux, see [Linux host compatibility](LINUX_COMPATIBILITY.md) for missing libraries or sandbox restrictions.

To use R, install it separately, for example with [rig](https://github.com/r-lib/rig#id-installation) and `rig add release`.
Python and SQL also work without R.
The first session may download Python and packages.

### Build from source

To install the development version, follow [Build from source](BUILD_FROM_SOURCE.md).

## Connect your client

Console runs on the same host as the client.
Start both in the project where the agent will work, so their shell and filesystem tools refer to the same files.

For Codex:

```sh
codex mcp add console -- mcp-console serve
```

For Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport stdio console -- mcp-console serve
```

For another MCP client, configure a stdio server with command `mcp-console` and arguments `["serve"]`.
Clients using an `mcpServers` mapping can use:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "console": {
      "command": "mcp-console",
      "args": ["serve"]
    }
  }
}
```

For remote work, run both Console and the client on the remote host.
Console does not manage remote connections or containers.

## Try an analysis

Ask your agent:

> Use MCP Console to generate a small dataset with NumPy and pandas, fit a simple model, and plot the result.
> Keep the data and model for follow-up.

Then ask:

> Which observations does the model fit poorly?
> Show a plot and the path to the recorded session.

With R installed, try the Palmer Penguins data from `palmerpenguins`, summarize it with SQL, and plot it from Python.
See [Working with R, Python, and SQL](BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md) for examples.

## Choose permissions and an environment

The default sandbox permits host-file reads and private temporary writes, but not ordinary workspace writes or direct network access.
**It does not protect readable secrets.**

### Use the workspace profile {#allow-project-writes}

To let the agent save files in the project, create `.agents/console/config.yaml` in the directory where Console will start:

```yaml
sandbox:
  profile: workspace
```

The `workspace` profile uses Console's launch directory as the workspace, even if evaluated code later changes its working directory.
It permits the agent to create, edit, and delete ordinary files there, while keeping the workspace's `.git`, `.agents`, `.codex`, and `.aws` paths read-only, including when they do not yet exist.
Git metadata referenced by a worktree's or submodule's `.git` file is also protected.
For example, the agent can read `data.csv`, edit `analysis.py`, and save `plot.png`, but cannot change `.agents/console/config.yaml` or Git metadata.

Host-file reads remain allowed, private temporary storage remains writable, and direct network access remains restricted.
The profile does not change the separate permissions used for package preparation.

Without a profile, you can construct the same filesystem permissions explicitly:

```yaml
sandbox:
  filesystem:
    read_write: [.]
    read_only: [.git, .agents, .codex, .aws]
```

Here `.` and the metadata paths are relative to Console's launch directory.
This retains the same default host reads, private temporary storage, and restricted networking.
Additional filesystem settings can narrow or widen access; see [the workspace profile](SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md#workspace-profile) for rule precedence and protecting other paths such as `.claude`.

For a write grant supplied by the client command instead of project configuration, add `--writable-root .`:

```sh
mcp-console serve --writable-root .
```

For a client using the JSON configuration above, the arguments become `["serve", "--writable-root", "."]`.
The flag adds a writable path; it does not select the workspace profile.
[Sandbox configuration](SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md#filesystem) describes metadata defaults and narrower grants.

Project configuration can select executables and widen permissions.
Review it before opening an unfamiliar project; `--no-project-config` skips that layer.

### Use an existing Python environment

To use a project's environment instead of a Console-managed one, add this to the configuration:

```yaml
python: .venv
```

The environment must already exist.
Ordinary Python and standard-library code do not require pandas, NumPy, or other optional data packages.
Install any third-party packages your analysis uses before starting the session; Console does not manage Python package installation for an environment selected this way.

Plotting and the default Python-owned DuckDB connection need their corresponding packages.
See [Python environment selection](CONFIGURATION.md#python-environment-selection) for interpreter requirements and [Packages and environments](REQUIREMENTS.md) for the distinction between managed and existing environments.

## Keep the session

Console records transcripts and artifacts locally.
[Recordings and reports](RECORDING.md) explains where to find them and how to turn a reviewed copy into a report.

Recordings are not checkpoints.
They contain input and output without redaction and are not automatically deleted.
